content.summary_of_the_review:
I really do not see anything new in this paper.  The heat maps are existent when computing joint positions using conventional GCN  and only when put into a graph structure do we lose that preciseness.    It appears that the paper also defines a precise location and then blurs that location.  Rather than processing as a graphical network, I assume that the paper treats the heat maps through time and processes these for action recognition, this does not appear to be anything new.
The idea appears to be trivial and does not differentiate itself enough from what actually exists in the literature.  The blueness of the joint positions appears to be arbitrary and does not correlate with the uncertainty in the joint position detection.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper17 by Reviewer aEYZ

content.title: Clarifications for Reviewer aEYZ
content.comment:
First of all, for **Novelty And Significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel**: 

We are the first to represent human skeletons as 3D heatmap volumes for action recognition and process them with 3D-CNN. Besides, we achieve competitive performance, surpass the GCN state-of-the-art across main benchmarks. Note that there have been hundreds of GCN papers for skeleton-based action recognition published, yet our PoseConv3D is comparable with the best of them. We **do not** agree with aEYZ's comments on either the **Technical Novelty And Significance** or the **Empirical Novelty And Significance** of this work. 

For issues in the main review:

1. I assume that GCN is defined as only coordinate based however there are methods out there that define them as heat maps as well and can be used for action recognition.
    1. This work lies in the scope of skeleton-based action recognition, while all previous works using GCN are coordinate-based. The two works you mentioned are **irrelated** works. There is **no** previous work showing the effectiveness of heatmap-based GCN for skeleton-based action recognition. 

2.  The 3D spoken of in this paper is the temporal definition as opposed to the 3rd spatial dimension which is a bit misleading. I know this is not explicitly and clearly stated at the beginning of the paper.
    1. **3D** in "PoseConv3D" indicates that the input takes **3D** heatmap volumes as inputs. The 3 dimensions are **Temporal Length, Height, Width**. That usage is very common in video understanding literature.

3. I am a bit confused, are all the heat maps through time converged into one heat map?
    1. No. For each shape, the heatmap volume is of shape **K x T x H x W**. 4 dimensions correspond to: 1) The number of keypoints; 2) The temporal length of the clip; 3) Height; 4) Width, which is clearly presented in the paper. Besides, the code for generating heatmap volumes is included in the supplementary materials.

4. What is the pre-processing described in the figure 2 caption? 
    1. Preprocessing includes **Subjects-centered Cropping** and **Uniform Sampling**, which is described in Sec 3.2. Specifically, we provide an example in Appendix Sec 2.

5. The heat maps spoken of in this paper have nothing to do with the uncertainty in determining the joint coordinates and positions but rather a definite location that is blurred by a gaussian, equation 1, at least it appears that way. 
    1. The main purpose of representing skeleton sequences as 3D heatmap volumes is to fit the 3D-CNN architecture. Besides, we also compared using gaussian maps or real heatmaps in Appendix 4.1, while the improvement of using real heatmaps is marginal.

6. For the experimentation, all the datasets used, it is not clear which ones are the authors and which ones belong to others, please properly address this with citations and clear statements.
    1. All video datasets are collected by previous works, except that we extract the human skeletons from these videos with practices proposed in this work. For all experiments we conducted, we adopt the human skeletons extracted by ourselves (**clearly stated in Sec 4.1**). In Table 3, when comparing with other prior works, we directly compare with the results reported in these papers (they obtain human skeletons in a different way). However, for the state-of-the-art MS-G3D, we also report the results of **MS-G3D + our human skeletons**. The results show that PoseConv3D outperforms the state-of-the-art GCN approach in a fair comparison (using the same human skeletons). 

7. The granularity of the action categories will bias the results. It would have been helpful to properly define what the classes are for the various test data sets and how many classes there are. 
    1. The action classes are defined in previous works which propose these datasets. 

For comments in **Summary Of The Review**:

1. I assume that the paper treats the heat maps through time and processes these for action recognition, this does not appear to be anything new. 
    1. We are the **first** to represent human skeletons as 3D heatmap volumes for action recognition and process them with 3D-CNN. Please list some references if you think **"this does not appear to be anything new"**. 

2. The idea appears to be trivial and does not differentiate itself enough from what actually exists in the literature. 
    1. We differentiate our work with other heatmap-related methods like PA3D or PoTion in **Related Works**, and demonstrate the advantage of our approach in Sec 4.3. 

3. The blueness of the joint positions appears to be arbitrary and does not correlate with the uncertainty in the joint position detection.
    1. What is **blueness**? Do you mean blurness? $\sigma$ is just a hyper-parameter when generating the pseudo heatmaps, that is not related to the uncertainty. Please check Eqn.1 and Eqn.2 in our paper.

replying_to: Replying to Revisiting Skeleton-based Action Recognition
display_title: Official Review of Paper17 by Reviewer CLvT

content.summary_of_the_paper:
- While most works in Skeleton based action recognition have used GCNs for modeling, this paper makes a case for using 3D CNNs instead. To do so, the paper represents the input as a stack of heatmaps instead of a joint graph. 3D CNNs popular in the RGB action recognition community are adopted for 3D stacked heatmaps. 
- The paper shows the advantages of the 3D CNNs over GCNs through extensive experiments. The proposed approach outperforms previous approaches on 6 skeleton-action recognition datasets and on fusion with RGB based approaches. Various properties of the approach and design choices are throughly analysed.
content.main_review:
Pros:
- The paper is well written and the problem being tackled is clearly described. The claims are supported by experiments. 
- Use of a 3D stack of heatmaps with standard 3D CNN backbones is a reasonable choice. The paper makes small modifications to the original architectures (like SlowFast, X3D) to account for the differences in RGB vs pose-heatmaps. In addition to bringing performance improvements, it often comes with reduced computational complexity. Also, the proposed approach is more scalable as number of people in the scene increase. 
- The study on various pose extractors and their effect on the final performance is helpful. 
- Good tricks and techniques : The paper uses certain tricks to further enhance the performance, some of which are borrowed from prior works in Skeletal-based action recognition and RGB-based action recognition to improve performance. Specifically, instead of uniform sampling, the paper uses the TSN style sampling to better cover the video content, to save on space coordinates are expanded into heatmaps during training, subject-centered cropping is performed to focus on the person in the frame, bidirectional lateral connections for multimodal fusion. 
- The study on performance, robustness and generalization of the proposed approach including experiments in the Appendix are helpful. 
- The approach does not require changing the architecture and hyperparameters for different datasets compared to other competing approaches. 
- The proposed approach can be used for multimodal early fusion more easily compared to prior approaches. 

Cons / Questions:
- The approach is not very novel and parts of the approach do exist in prior works in Skeleton & RGB based action recognition. That said, I think that the paper presents a good study on some of the best practices for Skeleton-based action recognition and makes a compelling case for using 3D CNNs for the task.  
- Pose Extractors :
    - It would help to include the pose extractor used (or GT) and whether 3D/2D skeletons were used in Table 3. 
    - It seems MS-G3D uses GT (provided with the dataset) skeleton, whereas the proposed approach and MS-G3D++ use 2D estimated skeletons. Does the paper claim that 2D estimated poses for NTU dataset give performance comparable or better than 3D GT skeletons (Table 3) ? Some intuitions on why this should be the case should help. 
    - While it is helpful to include the MS-G3D++ baseline for a fair comparison, a comparison with PoseConv3D using the heatmaps/poses used by prior approaches will further help separate the contribution of the pose extractor and the proposed model. 
- Multimodal fusion :
    - Since the various previous approaches might have different underlying models, the authors should also include R and P only results using their approach to Table 4. 
- A table which shows the contribution of each technique (sampling, subject-cropping) would be beneficial to understand the improvement in results over prior approaches (in context of Table 3). 
- Are the numbers in Figure 3 and Table 3 comparable ? 
- Does uniform sampling help GCN (like MS-G3D++) based approaches ? 
- 10-clip testing : 
    - It seems that the Table 3 results involve 10-clip testing. This should be mentioned in 'Skeleton-based Action Recognition' in 4.2. 
    - For 10-clip testing, are the prediction scores averaged for each of the sampled clips ? 

Minor / Other questions:
- Does Late fusion involve averaging the scores or does it involve training ? What about Early+Late fusion ? 
- The proposed approach scales more easily as the number of people in the scene increases as rightly pointed out. Would it hurt to have too many people since the heatmaps can merge into each other (clutter) whereas GCNs might not face this problem? What are your thoughts on this ? 
- Clarity : 
    - 3.2, 'target heatmap' can get confusing. 
    - I believe that the meaning of a 10-clip testing here is different from that used in some Action recognition setups where one crops from corners, center and applies flips to generate 10 clips. This should be clarified to avoid confusion. 

References/Related Works: 
- Some relevant references : 
    - Mimetics: Towards Understanding Human Actions Out of Context (IJCV 2021)
    - MMTM: Multimodal Transfer Module for CNN Fusion (CVPR 2020)
    - Stronger, Faster and More Explainable: A Graph Convolutional Baseline for Skeleton-based Action Recognition (ACM MM 2020)
    - JOLO-GCN: Mining Joint-Centered Light-Weight Information for Skeleton-Based Action Recognition (WACV 2021)
    - Dynamic Motion Representation for Human Action Recognition (WACV 2020)
- Some references which could be considered contemporaneous (which are probably not published, but atleast one arXiv version was available for >4 months). It would be good to include these but I wouldn't penalize this paper for not including them. 
    - IntegralAction: Pose-driven Feature Integration for Robust Human Action Recognition in Videos (arxiv April 2021 version) 
    - Pose And Joint-Aware Action Recognition (arXiv Oct 2020 version)
    - Quo Vadis, Skeleton Action Recognition? (arXiv Apr 2021 version)
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper is an empirical one and argues in favor of using 3D convolutions to model skeleton based action recognition. The paper provides extensive experiments for that and interesting observations and analysis showing the advantages of the proposed approach. 
There are a few potential issues detailed in the previous section. Considering all the pros and cons pointed out in Main review, my current rating is 6.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper17 by Reviewer CLvT

content.title: Some Clarifications for Reviewer CLvT
content.comment:
Thanks for the comments. We will polish the paper corresponding to this review. Below we address some concerns raised in the review.

### Cons / Questions

1. Pose Extractors:
    1. No GT poses are used for all entries in Table 3. For MS-G3D++ and PoseC3D, we use 2D human skeletons extracted with practices proposed in this work. For all other entries: 1) 3D skeletons collected with Kinect-v1 are used for NTURGB+D; 2) 2D skeletons extracted with OpenPose are used for Kinetics; 3) The previous pose extraction details are unknown for FineGYM (not mentioned in the paper). 

    2. Actually, the so-called **GT** 3D skeletons are not ground-truth, they are collected with Kinect-V1 sensors. We argue that actually, the 3D skeletons, either collected with sensors or estimated with SOTA pose estimators, are of low quality and achieve inferior performance in action recognition (discussed in Introduction, Figure 1; quantitative results in Appendix A 4.1).

    3. You can find that experiment in Appendix A 4.3, Table 16. PoseConv3D adopts 3D skeletons used in prior works (by projecting them to the image plane). If both use 2D skeletons as input, PoseConv3D outperforms the GCN-based counterpart by 2.4%, even surpasses
the MS-G3D with 3D skeletons as input by 0.4%: the spatiotemporal modeling capability of 3D-CNN can compensate for the information lost in the 3D → 2D projection.

2. Multimodal fusion: 
    For multimodal fusion results (Table 4(b)), we directly fuse our **P** results with the predictions of the state-of-the-art (VideoSwin and Omni-Source). The **P** results for K400, UCF, HMDB are listed in Table 3 and Table 15. 

3. A table that shows the contribution of each technique (sampling, subject-cropping) would be beneficial (in the context of Table 3).
    The contributions of these techniques are proved in the ablation study, and the improvements of these techniques are similar on all benchmarks. Table 3 is for comparisons with the state-of-the-art. 

4. Are the numbers in Figure 3 and Table 3 comparable?
    No. The clip length is 32 in Figure 3, 48 in Table 3. 

5. Does uniform sampling help GCN (like MS-G3D++) based approaches?
    We haven't conducted such experiments. We think it digresses a little from this work and can be studied in future works. 

6. 10-clip testing: 
    1. The Table 3 results do involve 10-clip testing. We will mention this in Sec 4.2. 
    2. They are averaged.

### Minor / Other questions
1. Late fusion involves averaging the scores of 2 separately trained models for 2 modalities. Early fusion involves the training: early-stage feature fusion happens when we jointly train the RGB model and Pose model. 

2. Based on existing experiments, we do not observe such a phenomenon. When there exist a dozen people, PoseConv3D still outperforms GCN-based approaches with much fewer parameters and FLOPs. We will conduct experiments to study if PoseConv3D can handle scenarios with lots of people (dozens to hundreds) in future works. However, we think such scenarios rarely occur in the context of action recognition. 

3. In Action Recognition literature, **10-clip testing** refers to aggregating predictions of 10 temporal clips. The practice you mentioned is called "10-crop testing". During revision, we will specify that means 10 temporal clips. 

### References/Related Works

All the references will be added to the paper during revision.

display_title: Official Review of Paper17 by Reviewer Ao4Q

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper addresses the problem of human action recognition. The proposed pipeline is composed of three modules:
- people detection
- 2d pose estimation
- action classification with CNN
The novelty is in the input of the third module, which is the 4D tensor (T x K x H x W) composed by the temporal stack of the K heatmaps, where K is the number of body joints. This data input allows the exploitation of CNN instead of GCN for the action classification step.
A very deep experimental section is provided to prove the superiority of the proposed data input.
content.main_review:
The main novelty of the submitted paper is the data input of the classification stage, which is the "stack" of the outputs from the previous stage. The novelty is thus limited.
Thus, in my opinion, the main contribution is the quality and quantity of experiments. 
However, experiments alone are not sufficient for this type of publication. Moreover, a more clear and structured evaluation should be reported. 
Follows a list of issues.

1) the keyword 3D is really misleading. The used poses are not 3d (x, y, z). The input of the classifier is not 3d but 4d (time x joint x H x W). 
2) The sentence "human skeleton is a compact representation of human action" is not true. Human skeleton is a representation of the instantaneous pose.
3) In the introduction: "feature representation: RGB frames, optical flows, audio waves, human skeletons". I think this is a collection of very different abstraction levels of data, and they are not only different representations
4) The issues of GCN approaches listed in the introduction should be used in the remain of the paper to prove the superiority of the proposed method. To this aim, I think that the robustness of the classification w.r.t. shift of coordinates should be better define and prove. Using top-down methods, coordinate normalization preprocessing tasks can solve the issue
5) "PoseConv3d can handle different numbers of persons wihtout increasing computational overhead" is not true nor demonstrated.
content.summary_of_the_review: The fundamental novelty claimed by the author is limited. Therefore, the significant part of the article could be a clear and precise experimental evaluation comparing the proposed solution with GCN ones. However, a lot of misleading sentences and corresponding experiments make the paper insufficient

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper17 by Reviewer Ao4Q

content.title: Some Clarifications for Reviewer Ao4Q
content.comment:
For issues in the main review: 

1. The keyword 3D is really misleading. 

    In this work, the **3D** in "PoseConv3D" indicates that the input takes **3D** heatmap volumes as inputs. The 3 dimensions are **Temporal Length, Height, Width**. That usage is very common in video understanding literature. Besides, it's proper to call the tensor "joint x time x H x W" **3D**, since "joint" corresponds to the channel number of the tensor. We think most people will call the tensor with shape "3 
 x H x W" as a 2D image (with 3 channels).

2.  The sentence "human skeleton is a compact representation of human action" is not true.

    The "human skeleton" here refers to the sequences of human skeletons. We think it's proper to call it a representation of human actions. 

3. I think this is a collection of very different abstraction levels of data, and they are not only different representations.

    The original sentence is: Existing studies have explored various modalities for feature representation, such as RGB frames, optical flow, audio waves, and human skeletons. 

     If you read it carefully, you will find that "RGB frames, optical flows, audio waves, human skeletons" correspond to **various modalities**, not **feature representation**. 

4.  I think that the robustness of the classification w.r.t. shift of coordinates should be better define and prove. 

     1. Dealing with missing keypoints is a common scenario in the real world, we think it's OK to use it to demonstrate the robustness of PoseConv3D. If you think there exist some better evaluation protocols, please share them with us. 

     2. We also design other experiments: like training/testing with skeletons extracted with different pose estimators to demonstrate the generalization capability of PoseConv3D. 

5. "PoseConv3d can handle different numbers of persons without increasing computational overhead" is not true nor demonstrated.

    The corresponding section in the original paper is Sec 4.4.3. In this example, we show that:

    1. For GCN, the input size grows linearly with the number of persons, which also makes the computation cost grow linearly.

    2. For PoseConv3d, since we can represent multiple persons without enlarging the input size (**we use one single heatmap volume to represent all 13 persons**), the computation cost is the same for different numbers of persons.


For **a lot of misleading sentences and corresponding experiments make the paper insufficient**: 

Please point out these "misleading sentences" and experiments you think are inefficient in the paper, we will appreciate your efforts and improve this work according to your comments.


Besides, we would like to reiterate the **novelty** of this work: we are the first to represent human skeletons as 3D heatmap volumes for action recognition and process them with 3D-CNN. Besides, we achieve competitive performance, surpass the GCN state-of-the-arts across main benchmarks. Note that there have been hundreds of GCN papers for skeleton-based action recognition published, yet our PoseConv3D is comparable with the best of them.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes to use a heatmap-based input representation for skeleton-based action recognition, instead of graph-based input which has been the popular choice in recent years. Heatmap-based input, combined with Conv3D prediction network, has several advantages such as its robustness and generalizability. The authors empirically demonstrates that the proposed approach achieves superior performance on standard benchmark datasets.
content.main_review:
Strength)
Experimentally shows that an alternative representation of heatmap input + 3DConv outperforms the popular graph-based approaches for skeleton-based action recognition task.
Proposed method is intuitive, simple, and shows robustness and better generalization ability as claimed by the authors.
Experimental evaluation is extensively done.

Weakness)
The 3DConv network framework itself is trivial. 
The claim on generalizability, as they put “we empirically find that PoseConv3D generalizes well across input skeletons obtained by different approaches.”, is quantitatively evaluated, but not well explained, persuasive or analyzed otherwise.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Overall)
Experimental findings from this paper is encouraging and promising. Researchers have spent much effort on improving GCN based models and while 3DConv based approaches were under-explored. Meanwhile, the paper currently lacks insights or further explanations on why this approach is much more robust and generalizable, other than the mere numbers. Overall, above borderline.
